Jewish marriage, called kiddushin, is a covenant between two partners sanctified by Jewish law and ritual. The core ritual is enacted when the groom presents an object of value to the bride while making a declaration: "Behold, you are consecrated to me with this ring, according to the law of Moses and Israel." This acquisition of the bride is what makes the marriage legally valid.

The ketubah, the marriage contract, is signed by two witnesses and read aloud before the couple, spelling out each partner's rights and responsibilities. The bride circles the groom under the chuppah, the wedding canopy, or in more modern egalitarian ceremonies, both partners circle each other. The canopy symbolizes the creation of a new home.

Seven blessings called sheva brachot are recited during or after the main ceremony, blessing the couple and invoking divine presence. At the ceremony's conclusion, the groom breaks a glass. This tradition is often interpreted as remembering the destruction of the Temple amidst joy, a way of acknowledging sorrow even in celebration. Some interpret it instead as symbolizing the fragility of human relationships.

Two valid witnesses must be present throughout the kiddushin and the ketubah signing. In Orthodox practice, they must be observant Jewish men. The ceremony is typically held in a public setting, affirming the marital bond before the community. A festive meal called a seudah follows, and the couple traditionally begins seven days of celebration during which the sheva brachot are repeated each evening.

The marriage represents a legal bond as well as a spiritual and emotional one. The ketubah itself, as a written contract, can be consulted if questions arise about the couple's obligations to each other. In Jewish tradition, marriage is understood not merely as a personal commitment but as a legal agreement recognized and validated by the Jewish community and by Jewish law.
